tours.title: Inner Harbour
tours.subtitle: Victoria's postcard icons all together
tours.about: Many people say that Victoria is the prettiest city in Canada. The Inner Harbour is a big reason for that.

stops.title: Victoria Visitor Centre
stops.summary: We start on the Visitor Centre terrace — the perfect spot to orient yourself and look around the harbour.
stops.transcript: Welcome to Victoria's Inner Harbour, the city's picturesque waterfront and one of Canada's most celebrated urban landscapes. From this panoramic viewpoint, admire the grand Empress Hotel, the Parliament Buildings and the small harbour. Your journey begins with a look at the landmarks that we'll soon be visiting - and that transformed this small coastal settlement into a world-famous destination.

stops.title: Fairmont Empress Hotel
stops.summary: Victoria's most iconic building isn't just a hotel — it's a carefully staged idea. Tea time, anyone?
stops.transcript: Opened in 1908, the Fairmont Empress Hotel was built by the Canadian Pacific Railway to transform Victoria into a fashionable tourist destination. Discover how engineers constructed this enormous hotel on unstable, reclaimed land, and why its architecture was designed to evoke the grandeur of an English manor house. Hear about its famous afternoon tea, its connection to trans-Pacific steamships and the enormous renovations that stripped away its iconic ivy. Behind the elegant façade lies a fascinating story of ambition, engineering and carefully cultivated British charm.

stops.title: Causeway Promenade
stops.summary: Victoria's postcard moment: boats, buskers, sea planes, and a photo opportunity every ten seconds.
stops.transcript: Follow the lower causeway promenade around the harbour, enjoying some of Victoria's finest waterfront views. This scenic walkway was part of an ambitious early-20th-century project that reshaped the shoreline and helped establish Victoria as a tourism destination. As you walk, listen to an excerpt from Sunshine City, a 1936 promotional film that captures how Victoria presented itself to visitors nearly a century ago. Enjoy the historic atmosphere, harbour scenery and a glimpse of the city's tourism heyday.

stops.title: Steamship Terminal
stops.summary: What is a fake Greek temple doing here? Discover how the terminal broadcast Britishness.
stops.transcript: Built in 1924 for the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Steamship Terminal once welcomed passengers travelling aboard the company's coastal steamships. Admire its classical architecture before looking out across a harbour that has been a centre of Indigenous activity, trade and transportation for thousands of years. Discover the surprising story of the sea otter fur trade, when these small marine mammals became valuable enough to fuel international rivalries between empires. A nearby monument commemorates the 1825 Anglo-Russian Treaty, connecting Victoria's waterfront to a much larger story of Pacific exploration and commerce.

stops.title: James Douglas, Sequoia Tree & Queen Victoria
stops.summary: Meet a teenage fur trader, a Gold Rush-era sequoia, and a thirty-foot Queen tucked behind a tree.
stops.transcript: Three landmarks on the Parliament grounds reveal fascinating connections between Victoria's colonial history, its natural landscape and the British Empire. Meet James Douglas, the Guyana-born fur trader who established Fort Victoria in 1843 and became British Columbia's first colonial governor. Discover how giant sequoias from California became fashionable additions to Victoria's landscape during the gold-rush era. Finally, admire the statue of Queen Victoria, the city's namesake, and hear how a dispute over its placement left the sculptor so furious that he refused to attend the unveiling.

stops.title: Legislative Assembly of BC
stops.summary: A statement of permanence built in 1898 — plus dark gossip about architect Francis Rattenbury.
stops.transcript: Completed in 1898, British Columbia's Parliament Buildings were designed to project the permanence, power and prestige of a young province. Their architect, Francis Rattenbury, was just 25 years old when he won the design competition, launching a spectacular career that would produce other famous buildings on this tour. Admire the Parliament Buildings' magnificent stonework, copper domes and golden statue of Captain George Vancouver. Then discover the astonishing personal story of Rattenbury himself, whose rise from obscurity to architectural fame ended in a scandalous affair and tragedy.

stops.title: Thunderbird Park
stops.summary: Totem poles, Indigenous history, and BC logging — a cedar museum that is history.
stops.transcript: Established in 1941, Thunderbird Park is an outdoor gallery of monumental Indigenous carvings representing the artistic traditions of several Northwest Coast nations. Meet Mungo Martin, the Kwakwaka'wakw artist and hereditary chief who helped revitalize Indigenous carving traditions after beginning a remarkable new chapter of his career in his seventies. Discover how totem poles preserve family histories, identities and cultural knowledge, and why their public display contrasted sharply with the restrictions Indigenous peoples faced at the time. You'll also learn about western red cedar, the extraordinary "Tree of Life" that sustained Indigenous communities for generations and later became central to British Columbia's logging industry.

stops.title: Emily Carr Statue
stops.summary: A woman, a dog, and a monkey — meet Victoria's best-known artist.
stops.transcript: Beside the Inner Harbour stands a bronze statue of Emily Carr, accompanied by her dog and a rather unusual companion: a monkey in a dress named Woo. Born and raised in Victoria, Carr defied the expectations of her era to become one of Canada's most celebrated painters and writers. Discover how her travels through British Columbia's forests and Indigenous communities inspired her bold artistic vision, and why she struggled for decades before finally achieving recognition in her fifties. Her remarkable journey from struggling artist to national icon provides a fitting conclusion to your exploration of Victoria's Inner Harbour.

tours.title: Old Town
tours.subtitle: From Fort Victoria to modern tourism district
tours.about: Brick façades, narrow alleys, and harbour commerce reveal a neighbourhood shaped by gold-rush urgency and reinvention.

stops.title: Introduction & Old Victoria Hotel
stops.summary: Get started on Victoria's historic main street and see a remarkable 1858 structure that survived an explosion.
stops.transcript: Begin your Old Town adventure on Government Street, the historic heart of Victoria. Discover one of British Columbia's oldest brick buildings, originally constructed as the Victoria Hotel in 1858, the year the Fraser River Gold Rush transformed the city. Hear the bizarre story of a hotel owner whose search for a gas leak ended in an explosion. And learn why this frontier-era brick building was later disguised as a quaint English cottage.

stops.title: Rogers’ Chocolates Shop
stops.summary: Meet Victoria's most famous chocolate shop and step inside the most beautiful historic store interior in the city.
stops.transcript: In 1885, Charles Rogers arrived in Victoria and opened a grocery store, only to discover that chocolates were his real calling. Together with his wife Leah, he built a thriving confectionery business whose signature Victoria Cream became a local favourite. Explore the beautifully preserved Edwardian shop, complete with original mahogany cabinets, stained glass and brass fittings. Along the way, discover a cracked glass counter, a secret peephole and the story behind one of Victoria's most beloved souvenirs.

stops.title: Old Victoria Customs House
stops.summary: Discover how a grand Customs House helped regulate Victoria's booming trade and gold rush migrations.
stops.transcript: Overlooking Victoria's Inner Harbour stands a striking salmon-pink building that once served as the city's federal Customs House. Opened in 1875, it regulated international trade, collected duties and reflected Victoria's emergence as a major Pacific port. During the Klondike Gold Rush, prospectors gathered here to obtain mining licences before heading north. Discover the building's elaborate French-inspired architecture, its original appearance and the story behind its unexpected pink makeover.

stops.title: Traces of Fort Victoria
stops.summary: Follow the traces of a fur-trading fort and pass by a very fine, poetic pub.
stops.transcript: A line of named bricks beneath your feet traces the boundaries of Fort Victoria, established by the Hudson's Bay Company in 1843. Discover how this cedar-walled trading post became the centre of a settlement transformed by the Fraser River Gold Rush. Look for the original fort gate markers and uncover the stories of early settlers, Indigenous peoples and pioneers commemorated in the pavement. You'll also meet a Polish-Jewish entrepreneur and a bank clerk who became a world-famous poet.

stops.title: Munro’s, Murchie’s & Morris
stops.summary: Discover three famous shops, from a Nobel Prize-winning novelist's bookstore to royal tea and an elegant tobacco shop.
stops.transcript: This stretch of Government Street brings together three of Victoria's most distinctive heritage businesses. Visit Munro's Books, housed in a magnificent former bank and co-founded by a Nobel Prize-winning author. Next door, discover Murchie's Tea & Coffee and its founder's questionable claims about supplying Queen Victoria's favourite tea. Finally, admire the remarkable onyx entrance and preserved Edwardian details of the former E.A. Morris tobacco shop.

stops.title: Bank of Montreal Building
stops.summary: Meet a grand 1897 bank, Victoria's most famous architect, and the manufactured tradition of the Irish Pub.
stops.transcript: The magnificent stone building now housing the Irish Times Pub began life as the Bank of Montreal in 1897. Designed by Francis Rattenbury, the architect behind Victoria's Parliament Buildings and Empress Hotel, its castle-like architecture projected wealth and authority. Today, the building offers a different kind of cultural experience: the modern Irish pub. Discover how Guinness helped turn the traditional Irish pub into a global export, and why this Victorian landmark makes such an interesting home for one.

stops.title: Bastion Square & Black Pioneers
stops.summary: Learn the remarkable story of a group Black Pioneers who migrated to Victoria in the 1850s seeking opportunity, freedom and equality.
stops.transcript: Between 1858 and 1860, several hundred Black Americans left California for Vancouver Island, encouraged by Governor James Douglas's promises of greater rights and opportunities. Discover their stories through the names embedded in the pavement near Bastion Square, including entrepreneurs, farmers, restaurateurs and community leaders. Meet Wellington Moses, who sold his own hair tonic in the Cariboo goldfields, and Mifflin Wistar Gibbs, who became a pioneering Black elected official. Their experiences reveal both the opportunities and the persistent discrimination that shaped early Victoria.

stops.title: Waddington Alley
stops.summary: Walk along century-old wooden paving stones and meet the ambitious businessman whose grandest scheme ended in disaster.
stops.transcript: Waddington Alley is one of Victoria's most atmospheric heritage passages, famous for its unusual wooden paving blocks dating to 1908. Named after Alfred Waddington, the alley was once a bustling commercial corridor packed with shops, workshops and entertainment venues. But Waddington's ambitions extended far beyond this little street: he dreamed of building a shortcut to the Cariboo goldfields. Discover how his speculative road project collapsed amid conflict with the Chilcotin people, leaving behind a legacy far darker than the charming alley that bears his name.

stops.title: Lower Johnson Street
stops.summary: Discover how a row of colourful Victorian storefronts survived demolition to become one of Victoria's most photogenic streets.
stops.transcript: Welcome to Lower Johnson Street, or LoJo, where a remarkable collection of 19th-century buildings now glows with bright colours. Once home to clothing merchants, grocers, hotels and other businesses, these storefronts reflect Victoria's close commercial and architectural connections with San Francisco. In the 1980s, heritage-minded developers helped rescue the aging buildings and gave many of them their distinctive new colours. And discover why this charming block preserves a surprisingly rare glimpse of the Victorian-era West Coast.

stops.title: Market Square
stops.summary: Discover how two  brothers transformed a city block into a heritage marketplace and glimpse the edge of Victoria's early Chinatown.
stops.transcript: Market Square looks like a historic courtyard, but its transformation into a pedestrian marketplace dates to the 1970s. Brothers Sam and Nick Bawlf rescued 14 aging buildings and turned a neglected block into a lively centre for shopping, dining and public life. Beneath the square lies the story of an old ravine that once divided Victoria's European commercial district from Chinatown. You'll also meet Lee Mong Kow, an influential Chinese Canadian interpreter and community leader whose family once lived in the buildings surrounding the square.

stops.title: Fan Tan Alley
stops.summary: Squeeze through the famously narrow Fan Tan Alley and uncover a hidden world of gambling, opium, commerce and community in historic Chinatown.
stops.transcript: At its narrowest point, Fan Tan Alley measures just 90 centimetres across, making it one of Victoria's most unusual and photogenic landmarks. But behind today's boutiques and cheerful lights lies a fascinating history of gambling dens, police raids, secret passageways and opium production. Discover how the alley developed as Chinatown grew denser, producing its distinctive architecture and curious half-numbered addresses. This final historical stop reveals a side of Victoria shaped by Chinese entrepreneurship, everyday community life and the challenges of racial discrimination.
